Heterogeneous Graph Setting. We consider a heterogeneous graph [ 62 ] 𝒢 = ( 𝒱 , ℰ , ϕ , ψ ) \mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\phi,\psi) , where 𝒱 \mathcal{V} and ℰ \mathcal{E} denote the sets of nodes and edges, while ϕ : 𝒱 → Φ \phi:\mathcal{V}\to\Phi and ψ : ℰ → Ψ \psi:\mathcal{E}\to\Psi are node and edge type mapping functions respectively. For an edge e = ( u , v ) e=(u,v) , we interchangeably write its type as ψ ⁡ ( e ) \psi(e) or ψ ⁡ ( u , v ) \psi(u,v) . Each node u ∈ 𝒱 u\in\mathcal{V} is associated with a feature vector 𝐱 u \mathbf{x}_{u} . Because feature sizes vary by node type, all nodes of a given type t ∈ Φ t\in\Phi share a specific input dimension f t f_{t} , meaning 𝐱 u ∈ ℝ f ϕ ⁡ ( u ) \mathbf{x}_{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{f_{\phi(u)}} .
3.1 HetSheaf : A Sheaf-based framework for Heterogeneous data

Existing heterogeneous GNNs ( Figure 1 ) handle heterogeneity at the architectural level, often leading to increasingly specialised and parameter-heavy designs that scale with the number of entity types, making the treatment of heterogeneity tightly coupled. Instead, we adopt a representation-centric view by modifying the input structure to encode specific heterogeneous knowledge while preserving topological information. Unlike standard graphs, which assume a single shared feature space for all nodes, cellular sheaves naturally capture heterogeneous data through type-specific local vector spaces and restriction maps that preserve local structure while enabling coherent global message passing. Motivated by this perspective, we introduce HetSheaf ( Figure 1 ), a general framework for heterogeneous sheaf neural networks. Given a heterogeneous graph 𝒢 = ( 𝒱 , ℰ , ϕ , ψ ) \mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\phi,\psi) , it first preprocesses type-dependent node features 𝐱 \mathbf{x} into a common channel dimension 𝐳 \mathbf{z} , then infers a cellular sheaf whose restriction maps are conditioned on both features and type information, and finally applies a sheaf neural architecture for downstream prediction. More formally, a heterogeneous sheaf neural network consists of three components:

Type-aware preprocessing , which projects input features 𝐱 \mathbf{x} into a shared channel space 𝐳 \mathbf{z} . Because each node type may have a different number of feature channels, we use a linear layer with bias for each node type to project node features into a common number of input channels. This can be combined with the sheaf projection step of the SheafNN to create the heterogeneous sheaf cochain 𝐳 ∈ C 0 ​ ( 𝒢 , ℱ ) \mathbf{z}\in C^{0}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{F}) . The modified linear layer takes in the original feature channels f t f_{t} and outputs d ​ f df features as the node stalk projection. We follow [ 46 , 79 ] to generate the input feature types f f by using either all of the node feature types (type-0), only the feature of the node target type (type-1) or replacing all node features with one-hot vectors (type-2).
Heterogeneous sheaf inference , ( Figure 2 ) which predicts restriction maps conditioned on node features and type information.

Sheaf-based representation learning , which applies a sheaf neural encoder followed by a task-specific decoder or readout. We apply task-specific representations (e.g., ℓ 2 \ell_{2} normalisation [ 46 ] or JKNet-style concatenations [ 71 ] ) before the final predictions, as detailed in Section 3.2 .

Let 𝒫 \mathcal{P} denote the preprocessing module, 𝚽 \bm{\Phi} the sheaf predictor, ℳ \mathcal{M} a sheaf neural encoder, and 𝒟 \mathcal{D} a downstream decoder. The overall pipeline can be written abstractly as:

𝐳 u \displaystyle\mathbf{z}_{u} = 𝒫 ϕ ⁡ ( u ) ​ ( 𝐱 u ) \displaystyle=\mathcal{P}_{\phi(u)}(\mathbf{x}_{u}) (2) ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e ≔ ( u , v ) \displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e\coloneq(u,v)} = 𝚽 ⁡ ( 𝐳 u , 𝐳 v , ϕ ⁡ ( u ) , ϕ ⁡ ( v ) , ψ ⁡ ( e ) ) \displaystyle=\bm{\Phi}(\mathbf{z}_{u},\mathbf{z}_{v},\phi(u),\phi(v),\psi(e)) (3) 𝐲 ^ \displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{y}} = 𝒟 ⁡ ( ℳ ⁡ ( 𝒢 , ℱ , { 𝐳 u } u ∈ 𝒱 ) ) \displaystyle=\mathcal{D}\!\left(\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{F},\{\mathbf{z}_{u}\}_{u\in\mathcal{V}})\right) (4)

Since heterogeneity is encoded into the inferred sheaf itself, once the sheaf has been constructed, it can be processed by any sheaf-based neural architecture, including Neural Sheaf Diffusion [ 4 ] , Sheaf Attention Networks [ 3 ] , Polynomial Neural Sheaf Diffusion [ 5 ] or other sheaf variants, without requiring ad hoc heterogeneous redesign.
3.2 Heterogeneous Sheaf Predictors and Model Adaptations

Heterogeneous Sheaf Predictors. A key ingredient of HetSheaf is the explicit construction of restriction maps from heterogeneous information. In standard sheaf learning, restriction maps are predicted from node features alone as ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ ( u , v ) = 𝚽 ⁡ ( 𝐱 u , 𝐱 v ) \mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq(u,v)}=\bm{\Phi}(\mathbf{x}_{u},\mathbf{x}_{v}) . Although such a predictor may implicitly recover type-dependent behaviour, it does not explicitly exploit the typed structure available in heterogeneous graphs. We therefore parametrise the restriction maps so that the learned sheaf structure is conditioned on node features (projected into the shared channel via 𝒫 ϕ ⁡ ( ∗ ) \mathcal{P}_{\phi(*)} ), node and edge types as described in Eq 2 . Following [ 4 ] , we consider diagonal, orthogonal, and general restriction-map families (see more details in Section B.4.3 ), and we instantiate the heterogeneous sheaf through a family of heterogeneous sheaf predictors that vary along two axes. The former concerns which type signals are used : from no type information (Sheaf-NSD, where we only concatenate the projected information relative to the node features 𝐳 u , 𝐳 v \mathbf{z}_{u},\mathbf{z}_{v} ), to node-only ( HetSheaf-NE, HetSheaf-NT ) or edge-only ( HetSheaf-EE, HetSheaf-ET ) variants, up to predictors conditioned on both node and edge types ( HetSheaf-TE, HetSheaf-types, HetSheaf-ensemble ). The latter regards how type information is routed : most variants use a shared MLP with type indicators as additional inputs, whereas HetSheaf-ensemble allocates a separate predictor to each edge type MLP ψ ⁡ ( e ) \text{MLP}_{\psi(e)} , increasing expressivity at the cost of additional parameters. Figure 2 summarises the predictor family, while full details and complexity analyses are deferred to Section B.4.4 .

Attention Restriction Maps. A further design choice concerns how the raw output of 𝚽 \bm{\Phi} is converted into a restriction map. [ 4 ] formulate an alternative attention-style post-processing step. For the general case, a row-wise softmax yields row-stochastic restriction maps, and this transformation depends only on the output of 𝚽 \bm{\Phi} , and we can apply it uniformly to all HetSheaf variants:

ℱ u ​ ⊴ ​ e = 𝐈 d − Softmax ⁡ ( 𝚽 ⁡ ( 𝐳 u , 𝐳 v , ϕ ⁡ ( u ) , ϕ ⁡ ( v ) , ψ ⁡ ( e ) ) ) \mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}=\mathbf{I}_{d}-\mathrm{Softmax}\!\left(\bm{\Phi}(\mathbf{z}_{u},\mathbf{z}_{v},\phi(u),\phi(v),\psi(e))\right) (5)

Task-specific Preprocessing. Because different node types may have different input dimensionalities, we use a type-specific linear projection with bias 𝐳 u = 𝒫 ϕ ⁡ ( u ) ​ ( 𝐱 u ) , ∀ u ∈ 𝒱 \mathbf{z}_{u}=\mathcal{P}_{\phi(u)}(\mathbf{x}_{u}),\forall u\in\mathcal{V} to map all node features into a shared channel dimension. These projections are learned jointly with the rest of the model and can be combined with the initial stalk projection of the sheaf encoder to construct the input cochain 𝐳 ∈ C 0 ​ ( 𝒢 , ℱ ) \mathbf{z}\in C^{0}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{F}) . Following [ 46 , 79 ] , we consider multiple feature initialisation strategies, including using all available node features, target-type-only features, and one-hot type indicators. For node classification , we apply ℓ 2 \ell_{2} normalisation to the final node representation: 𝐨 u = 𝐡 u ( L ) ∥ 𝐡 u ( L ) ∥ \mathbf{o}_{u}=\frac{\mathbf{h}_{u}^{(L)}}{\lVert\mathbf{h}_{u}^{(L)}\rVert} , where 𝐡 u ( L ) \mathbf{h}_{u}^{(L)} is the final hidden state of node u u . For link prediction , we follow a JKNet-style strategy [ 71 ] and concatenate the normalised hidden states across layers: 𝐨 u = ∥ l = 1 L 𝐡 u ( l ) ∥ 𝐡 u ( l ) ∥ \mathbf{o}_{u}=\concat_{l=1}^{L}\frac{\mathbf{h}_{u}^{(l)}}{\lVert\mathbf{h}_{u}^{(l)}\rVert} .

Sheaf Models Adaptations. A key advantage of HetSheaf is its model-agnosticity: once a heterogeneous sheaf has been inferred, the resulting typed geometric structure can be processed by a broad class of existing sheaf neural architectures with minimal modifications. To demonstrate this property, we adapt both Sheaf Attention Networks (SheafAN) [ 3 ] and Polynomial Neural Sheaf Diffusion (PolyNSD) [ 5 ] to the heterogeneous setting. For SheafAN, we make the attention mechanism type-aware by augmenting the attention input with node-type and edge-type information. For PolyNSD, instead, we preserve the original polynomial spectral filtering scheme and apply it directly to the heterogeneous sheaf Laplacian p ⁡ ( L ℱ ) = ∑ k = 0 K c k ​ L ℱ k p(L_{\mathcal{F}})=\sum_{k=0}^{K}c_{k}L_{\mathcal{F}}^{k} , where L ℱ L_{\mathcal{F}} is now induced by the type-aware restriction maps learned by HetSheaf , allowing to perform higher-order diffusion directly over the heterogeneous sheaf without requiring any ad hoc redesign. Full model-specific derivations and implementation details are deferred to Sections B.4.6 and B.4.7 .
4 SheafPool : Stalk-Space Late-token Readout

Graph-level prediction is more delicate in sheaf neural networks than in standard GNNs. While relying on the common latent space assumption, for which we can apply a pooling hierarchy, sheaf node embeddings 𝐇 i ∈ ℝ d × C \mathbf{H}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times C} are meaningful only up to node-wise changes of basis.

Consequently, a valid graph readout must satisfy two requirements simultaneously: it must be permutation-invariant over nodes, and it must be compatible with stalk-wise gauge reparameterisations 𝐇 i ↦ 𝐆 i ​ 𝐇 i , 𝐆 i ∈ 𝔾 \mathbf{H}_{i}\mapsto\mathbf{G}_{i}\mathbf{H}_{i},\mathbf{G}_{i}\in\mathbb{G} , where 𝔾 \mathbb{G} denotes the gauge family induced by the restriction-map parameterisation (e.g. diagonal, orthogonal, or general invertible maps). However, the standard flatten-and-pool procedure on vec ⁡ ( 𝐇 i ) ∈ ℝ d ​ C \mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{H}_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{dC} does not satisfy this requirement: they depend on arbitrary stalk coordinates chosen for each stalk, so equivalent sheaf representations may produce different graph embeddings, (as also shown in Table 1 ). To address this issue, we introduce SheafPool , a Stalk-Space Late-token Readout graph pooling mechanism that first canonicalises node embeddings (i.e., maps to a common reference stalk frame), then aggregates them directly in stalk space, and only collapses the stalk dimension at the very end. The construction preserves the stalk geometry, while remaining applicable to all sheaf families.

Stalk-Space Late-Token Formalisation. Formally, we define a graph-level readout as ℛ : { 𝐇 i } i ∈ V g ⟼ 𝐠 g ∈ ℝ C \mathcal{R}:\{\mathbf{H}_{i}\}_{i\in V_{g}}\longmapsto\mathbf{g}_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} , whose output is permutation-invariant over nodes and robust to stalk reparameterisations. The readout consists in five stages that can be summarised ( fig. 3 ) as:

𝐇 i → whiten 𝐙 i → align 𝐙 ~ i → attn pool 𝐏 g → late token 𝐓 ^ g → energy 𝐠 g \mathbf{H}_{i}\xrightarrow{\text{whiten}}\mathbf{Z}_{i}\xrightarrow{\text{align}}\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{i}\xrightarrow{\text{attn pool}}\mathbf{P}_{g}\xrightarrow{\text{late token}}\widehat{\mathbf{T}}_{g}\xrightarrow{\text{energy}}\mathbf{g}_{g} (6)

(1) Per-node whitening. We first remove node-wise scaling and shearing in the stalk dimension by forming 𝐒 i = 𝐇 i ​ 𝐇 i ⊤ + ε ​ 𝐈 d \mathbf{S}_{i}=\mathbf{H}_{i}\mathbf{H}_{i}^{\top}+\varepsilon\mathbf{I}_{d} , and defining 𝐙 i = 𝐒 i − 1 / 2 𝐇 i \mathbf{Z}_{i}=\mathbf{S}_{i}^{-1/2}\mathbf{H}_{i} . This makes the stalk covariance approximately isotropic, thus reducing remaining ambiguity to an orthogonal transform.

(2) Anchor-based alignment. After whitening, different nodes may still be represented in different orthogonal frames. We therefore align each node to a shared learnable anchor 𝐀 ∈ ℝ d × C \mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times C} via 𝐑 i = arg ⁡ min 𝐑 ∈ O ⁡ ( d ) ⁡ ‖ 𝐑 ⊤ ​ 𝐙 i − 𝐀 ‖ F 2 \mathbf{R}_{i}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{R}\in O(d)}\|\mathbf{R}^{\top}\mathbf{Z}_{i}-\mathbf{A}\|_{F}^{2} , and set 𝐙 ~ i = 𝐑 i ⊤ ​ 𝐙 i \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{i}=\mathbf{R}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{Z}_{i} . This places all node embeddings in a common stalk frame before pooling.

(3) Invariant attention weights. To weight node contributions without using basis-dependent coordinates, we score each node through the channel-wise energies of its whitened representation 𝐮 i = diag ⁡ ( 𝐙 i ⊤ ​ 𝐙 i ) ∈ ℝ C \mathbf{u}_{i}=\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{Z}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{Z}_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{C} . Since 𝐮 i \mathbf{u}_{i} is invariant to residual orthogonal reparameterisations, a learnable scorer s θ s_{\theta} can produce graph-wise attention weights α i = exp ⁡ ( s θ ​ ( 𝐮 i ) ) ∑ j ∈ V g exp ⁡ ( s θ ​ ( 𝐮 j ) ) . \alpha_{i}=\frac{\exp(s_{\theta}(\mathbf{u}_{i}))}{\sum_{j\in V_{g}}\exp(s_{\theta}(\mathbf{u}_{j}))}.

(4) Stalk-space pooling with a late receive-only token. We then aggregate the aligned embeddings directly in stalk space 𝐏 g = ∑ i ∈ V g α i ​ 𝐙 ~ i ∈ ℝ d × C \mathbf{P}_{g}=\sum_{i\in V_{g}}\alpha_{i}\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times C} . To perform readout without inserting a token into the encoder during the diffusion process, which would cause oversmoothing, we use a late, receive-only token 𝐓 ∈ ℝ d × C \mathbf{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times C} updated only after pooling 𝐓 ^ g = ϕ ⁡ ( [ 𝐓 , 𝐏 g ] ) \widehat{\mathbf{T}}_{g}=\phi([\mathbf{T},\mathbf{P}_{g}]) , where ϕ \phi is a small channel-wise MLP with layer normalisation.

(5) Invariant graph feature extraction. Finally, we collapse the stalk dimension through channel-wise energies: 𝐠 g = diag ⁡ ( 𝐓 ^ g ⊤ ​ 𝐓 ^ g ) ∈ ℝ C \mathbf{g}_{g}=\mathrm{diag}(\widehat{\mathbf{T}}_{g}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{T}}_{g})\in\mathbb{R}^{C} . The resulting graph embedding is then fed to a standard MLP decoder for graph classification.

A.1 Problem Setting and Gauge Quotient Viewpoint
Let G g = ( V g , E g ) G_{g}=(V_{g},E_{g}) be a graph and let a sheaf neural encoder produce node embeddings:
𝐇 i ∈ ℝ d × C for i ∈ V g \mathbf{H}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times C}\quad\text{for}\quad i\in V_{g} (7)
where d d is the stalk dimension and C C is the channel dimension. For graph classification, the goal is to construct a readout that summarises the graph into a single graph representation:
ℛ : { 𝐇 i } i ∈ V g ↦ 𝐠 g ∈ ℝ C \mathcal{R}:\{\mathbf{H}_{i}\}_{i\in V_{g}}\mapsto\mathbf{g}_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} (8)

In ordinary GNNs, all node embeddings live in the same latent space, usually ℝ C \mathbb{R}^{C} . To obtain a graph-level representation, we can simply pool the set of node embeddings 𝐡 i , i ∈ V g {\mathbf{h}_{i}},{i\in V_{g}} using a permutation-invariant operation such as sum, mean, or max pooling. In a sheaf model, the situation is different: the hidden state of node i i lives in its own local vector space, called the stalk ℱ ⁡ ( i ) \mathcal{F}(i) . After choosing a basis for this stalk, the node state can be written as a matrix 𝐇 i ∈ ℝ d × C \mathbf{H}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times C} . However, this coordinate representation is not intrinsic: different nodes may use different bases, and there is generally no canonical basis shared by all stalks. Therefore, if we change the basis of the stalk ℱ ⁡ ( i ) \mathcal{F}(i) by a matrix 𝐆 i ∈ 𝔾 i ⊆ G ​ L ​ ( d ) \mathbf{G}_{i}\in\mathbb{G}_{i}\subseteq GL(d) , the same underlying sheaf signal is represented in different coordinates as:
𝐇 i ↦ 𝐇 i ′ := 𝐆 i ​ 𝐇 i with 𝐆 i ∈ 𝔾 \mathbf{H}_{i}\mapsto\mathbf{H}_{i}^{\prime}:=\mathbf{G}_{i}\mathbf{H}_{i}\quad\text{with}\quad\mathbf{G}_{i}\in\mathbb{G} (9)

where 𝔾 \mathbb{G} depends on the restriction-map family: a diagonal subgroup of G ​ L ​ ( d ) GL(d) in the diagonal case, O ⁡ ( d ) O(d) or a metric-preserving subgroup in the orthogonal/bundle case, and G ​ L ​ ( d ) GL(d) in the general case. We refer to this action as a local gauge action on the stalk.
Definition A.1 (Gauge Orbit) .
For a node embedding 𝐇 ∈ ℝ d × C \mathbf{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times C} , define its gauge orbit as:
[ 𝐇 ] 𝔾 := { 𝐆𝐇 : 𝐆 ∈ 𝔾 } [\mathbf{H}]_{\mathbb{G}}:=\{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{H}:\mathbf{G}\in\mathbb{G}\} (10)
A graph-level readout is gauge-invariant if it depends only on the multiset of node-wise gauge orbits.
Thus, a principled sheaf readout must satisfy two requirements simultaneously:
Permutation invariance over nodes: reordering the nodes of a graph must not change the output.
Gauge compatibility / invariance: equivalent local coordinate realisations of the same stalk signal must produce the same graph descriptor.
Definition A.2 (Gauge-compatible graph readout) .

Let 𝔾 := ∏ i ∈ V g 𝔾 i \mathbb{G}:=\prod_{i\in V_{g}}\mathbb{G}_{i} be the product of the admissible node-wise gauge groups, where 𝔾 i \mathbb{G}_{i} is determined by the restriction-map family (e.g. diagonal, orthogonal, or general invertible transforms). A graph-level readout
ℛ : { 𝐇 i } i ∈ V g ↦ 𝐠 g \mathcal{R}:\{\mathbf{H}_{i}\}_{i\in V_{g}}\mapsto\mathbf{g}_{g} (11)
is said to be gauge-compatible if

ℛ ⁡ ( { 𝐆 i ​ 𝐇 i } i ∈ V g ) = ℛ ⁡ ( { 𝐇 i } i ∈ V g ) ∀ ( 𝐆 i ) i ∈ V g ∈ 𝔾 , \mathcal{R}(\{\mathbf{G}_{i}\mathbf{H}_{i}\}_{i\in V_{g}})=\mathcal{R}(\{\mathbf{H}_{i}\}_{i\in V_{g}})\qquad\forall(\mathbf{G}_{i})_{i\in V_{g}}\in\mathbb{G}, (12)
and permutation-invariant if its value is unchanged under any reordering of the node index set V g V_{g} .
Remark .

In our implementation, gauge compatibility is achieved through a normalisation-and-alignment procedure, similar to [ 58 ] . We first apply node-wise whitening, which places each stalk representation in a normalised coordinate system and reduces general G ​ L ​ ( d ) GL(d) gauge freedom to a residual orthogonal ambiguity, namely, removes scale and shear effects. However, each whitened stalk may still differ by an orthogonal rotation or reflection. To make node representations comparable before pooling, we then align all whitened stalks to a common learnable reference, or anchor, by solving an anchor-based Procrustes problem. This step selects, for each node, the orthogonal transformation that best matches its whitened stalk representation to the anchor. Once all stalks are expressed in this shared aligned frame, we apply a permutation-invariant pooling operator to obtain the graph-level descriptor. This design makes the readout robust to local changes of basis. The invariance we obtain here is approximate in finite samples and may degrade when the stalk covariance matrices are ill-conditioned.
B.4.4 Full Description of Heterogeneous Sheaf Predictors

We next give the complete definition of the heterogeneous predictor family used in the experiments. These variants differ in two ways: first, in which typed signals are provided to the predictor (node features, node types, edge types, or combinations thereof), and second, in how this information is routed (shared predictor versus edge-type-specific ensemble). This family allows us to disentangle the contribution of feature-level conditioning from that of pure structural-type information.
